content: Although over-the-counter combination medications containing antihistamines, decongestants, and/or analgesics are widely used for the common cold, the evidence supporting their effectiveness is limited. This review, updated from its original publication in 2012, aimed to evaluate the efficacy of these combination treatments compared to placebo or other active treatments (excluding antibiotics) in reducing symptom duration and alleviating symptoms such as general malaise, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sneezing, and cough in both children and adults. The review included randomized controlled trials that assessed the effectiveness of these combination treatments. A total of 30 studies involving 6304 participants were identified, with 31 treatment comparisons. Most trials used placebo as the control, while a few used active substances such as paracetamol, diphenhydramine, or other combinations. The quality of reporting was generally poor, and there was significant variability in study design, participant demographics, interventions, and outcomes. Most studies involved adults, with only nine trials including children. Of these, three trials included very young children (6 months to 5 years), and five trials included children aged 2 to 16 years. The trials were conducted in various settings, including university clinics, pediatric departments, family medicine practices, and general practice surgeries. Antihistamine-Decongestant Combinations Fourteen trials (1298 participants) evaluated antihistamine-decongestant combinations. Eight trials reported on overall effectiveness, with six trials pooled for analysis. The odds ratio (OR) for treatment failure was 0.31 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.20 to 0.48), indicating moderate certainty evidence. The number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) was 3.9 (95% CI 3.03 to 5.2). On the final evaluation day (3 to 10 days of follow-up), 70% of participants receiving active treatment showed a favorable response compared to 55% in the placebo group. However, adverse effects were more common in the antihistamine-decongestant group (31% vs. 13%; OR 1.58, 95% CI 0.78 to 3.21). Antihistamine-Analgesic Combinations Four trials (1608 participants) assessed antihistamine-analgesic combinations. Two trials reported on overall effectiveness, with one trial providing data for analysis. The OR for treatment failure was 0.33 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.46), with moderate certainty evidence. The NNTB was 6.67 (95% CI 4.76 to 12.5). After six days of treatment, 70% of participants in the active treatment group were cured compared to 43% in the control group. Adverse effects, such as drowsiness and sleepiness, were not significantly more frequent in the active treatment group compared to placebo (10/152 vs. 4/120; OR 1.64, 95% CI 0.48 to 5.59). Analgesic-Decongestant Combinations Seven trials (2575 participants) evaluated analgesic-decongestant combinations. One trial reported on overall effectiveness, showing that 73% of participants in the active treatment group experienced benefit compared to 52% in the control group (OR for treatment failure 0.28, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.52; moderate certainty evidence). The NNTB was 4.7. However, adverse effects were significantly more common in the active treatment group (199/1122 vs. 75/675; OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.18 to 2.23), with a number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome (NNTH) of 17. Antihistamine-Analgesic-Decongestant Combinations Six trials (1014 participants) assessed antihistamine-analgesic-decongestant combinations. Five trials reported on overall effectiveness, with two studies in adults pooled for analysis. The OR for treatment failure was 0.47 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.67), with low certainty evidence. The NNTB was 5.6 (95% CI 3.8 to 10.2). However, the difference in global effect between active treatment and placebo was less than one point on a fouror five-point scale. One trial in children aged 2 to 12 years and two trials in adults found no significant benefit. Adverse effects were reported in one trial, with 2% of participants in the active treatment group and 4% in the placebo group experiencing adverse effects. Two other trials reported no differences in adverse effects between groups. Authors' Conclusions The evidence for the effectiveness of antihistamine-analgesic-decongestant combinations in treating the common cold is limited. The available data suggest that these combinations may provide some general benefit in adults and older children, but the effect on individual symptoms is likely too small to be clinically meaningful. These potential benefits must be weighed against the risk of adverse effects, which were more common in some treatment groups. There is no evidence to support the effectiveness of these combinations in young children. Additionally, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a warning in 2005 regarding adverse effects associated with over-the-counter nasal preparations containing phenylpropanolamine.
